answers.primary: A remote MCP server for the error-tracking vendor, connected over HTTP/SSE transport and authenticated with the vendor's OAuth browser flow so each engineer authorizes in their own browser and the resulting token is stored in that engineer's local Claude Code credential store. Configured once (user scope for personal use, or project scope in .mcp.json if the whole repo needs it) and authorized per person via /mcp.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that wraps the vendor's REST API behind curl calls in the Bash tool, keyed to a shared long-lived API token in an environment variable. Rejected because it reintroduces the shared static credential the requirement is trying to eliminate and gives no per-engineer identity or revocation.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code owns the transport, the OAuth handshake, token storage and refresh, and the tool-call permission prompts; the model only decides which of the exposed tools to call.
answers.context_boundary: The query executes inside the vendor's service and the MCP client process, entirely outside the model's window. What crosses into the main session context is the tool schema list at connect time and the JSON tool results the model requested; the access token itself never enters the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: The connection is established when a session starts with the server configured, and the OAuth grant happens once per engineer at first authorization and persists across sessions until the token expires or is revoked. It stops applying when the server is removed from config, when the grant is revoked vendor-side, or when the session ends.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthorized or expired grant means the tools simply are not offered or every call errors, and the model falls back to asking the engineer to paste again. The practical damage is context bloat, since issue and stack-trace payloads from an error tracker are large and land verbatim in the window, so the server should expose narrow filtered tools rather than a raw query passthrough.
answers.version_caveat: Remote MCP over HTTP with OAuth authorization is supported in current Claude Code, but I cannot state the exact minimum version or the precise CLI flag spelling from memory and will not invent one. Enterprise-managed settings can restrict which MCP servers are permitted, so a managed-policy deployment may block this regardless of the local config.

answers.primary: LSP integration: register a TypeScript language server so the harness attaches compiler diagnostics to the result of each edit and exposes definition and reference lookups as first-class navigation rather than text search. This is the mechanism whose whole purpose is post-edit diagnostics plus symbol navigation, so it should own the behaviour.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook running tsc --noEmit after every Edit or Write. It would deliver diagnostics deterministically, but it recompiles the project on every edit, is far too slow to sit in the edit loop, and does nothing at all for go-to-definition or find-references.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It launches and talks to the language server and attaches diagnostics to the tool result without the model asking; the model owns only whether it acts on what it is shown.
answers.context_boundary: The type check runs in the language server process outside the model's window. What crosses back is the diagnostic list scoped to the edited file, plus definition and reference locations when the model requests them, so the model sees errors instead of whole-project compiler output.
answers.lifecycle: The server starts when the session first touches a file of that language and stays warm for the session; diagnostics are delivered on every subsequent edit. It stops applying at session end, on files outside the server's project root, and for languages with no server configured.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Diagnostics are information, not a gate, so the model can read a type error and proceed anyway; the requirement here is really a hook or a CI check if the errors must actually block. A large TypeScript project also means tsserver takes tens of seconds to index, so early edits in a session may come back clean simply because the server was not ready, and a codebase with pre-existing errors floods each result with noise the model learns to skip.
answers.version_caveat: LSP support in Claude Code is a recent addition and I do not know its exact version gate, its configuration key name, or whether it is still flagged experimental, so I am not going to state one. If the installed version predates it, the fallback is a PostToolUse hook running an incremental tsc against the touched file.

answers.primary: A plugin published through a plugin marketplace. One plugin bundles the review skills and slash commands, the hooks that provide the edit-time automations, and the MCP server definition for the shared external tool; the marketplace and the enabled plugin are declared in each repository's checked-in .claude/settings.json so a fresh clone offers the same set, and updates flow from the marketplace repository.
answers.rejected_alternative: Copying the same .claude/skills, .claude/commands and hook entries into every repository directly. Rejected because there is no update path: every published change becomes a manual pull request against every repo and the copies drift within a week.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and that is the point of the design. The harness owns discovery, the trust prompt, installation and loading of the plugin's hooks and MCP entries; the model owns whether it actually invokes the skills and commands the plugin contributes.
answers.context_boundary: Each component crosses differently. Skill names and descriptions load into every session's window as lightweight metadata with the body pulled in only on invocation, commands enter only when invoked, MCP tool schemas enter at connect time, and hooks never enter the model's context at all because they run in the harness process.
answers.lifecycle: It becomes available the first time an engineer opens a repository whose settings declare the marketplace, after they accept the trust prompt for that source. It stays in force for every session in every repo carrying that declaration, and stops when the plugin is disabled, the marketplace entry is removed, or the engineer declines to trust it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on adoption and silently on updates. The trust prompt is declinable, so an engineer who says no simply has none of it and nothing tells the platform team; an unreachable marketplace means everyone quietly runs yesterday's version. The sharper risk is that a hook change ships to every engineer's machine with no per-repo review, so a bad edit-time automation blocks work fleet-wide.
answers.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are a comparatively recent Claude Code capability and the settings keys that declare a known marketplace and an enabled plugin exist, but I will not state the exact key spellings or a minimum version from memory. Managed enterprise policy can also restrict which marketplaces are installable.

answers.primary: Ship the binary inside the plugin and have the plugin put its executable directory on the PATH used for Bash tool invocations, so the CLI resolves as a bare command name in ordinary pipelines. Where the installed version does not contribute PATH automatically, the equivalent is the plugin shipping a settings fragment or a SessionStart hook that prepends the plugin root's bin directory to PATH for the session.
answers.rejected_alternative: An MCP server wrapping each subcommand as a discrete tool. Rejected because it defeats the actual requirement: MCP tool results come back as structured payloads to the model, so the CLI can no longer be composed with grep and jq inside a single shell pipeline, and a many-subcommand binary would flood the tool list.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It constructs the environment that the Bash tool inherits, so PATH contribution is a harness-level fact; the model just types a command name and either it resolves or it does not.
answers.context_boundary: The binary runs as a normal subprocess of the Bash tool, in the session's shell environment and not in the model's window. Only the command's stdout and stderr cross back, which is exactly why pipeline composition with grep and jq is valuable: filtering happens before anything reaches the context.
answers.lifecycle: It applies for the duration of any session in which the toolkit plugin is enabled, from the point the environment is constructed at session start. It stops when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, and it does not survive into shells the harness did not spawn.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and confusingly. If the PATH contribution does not take, the model gets a plain command not found and will usually improvise around it, often by inventing an absolute path or a different tool, rather than reporting the misconfiguration. A second trap is permission rules: allow entries written against the bare command name will not match if the model falls back to invoking the binary by absolute path, so it prompts on every call.
answers.version_caveat: I am not confident that plugins expose an automatic PATH contribution for bundled executables in the installed version, and I will not invent a manifest field name for it. The dependable fallback that I can vouch for conceptually is exporting PATH from a session-start hook or settings environment block using the plugin root variable; the binary must also be shipped per platform or fetched at install time, since a compiled binary is not portable across macOS, Linux and Windows.

answers.primary: Distribute the toolkit as a plugin from a git-backed marketplace that tracks a branch rather than tagged releases, so the source of truth is the default branch of the repository and every merged commit is what consumers resolve to on their next update. No version numbers, no changelog gate, no publish step.
answers.rejected_alternative: Publishing versioned artifacts, for example an npm package or tagged release tarballs, that consumers pin and bump. Rejected precisely because it is the release bookkeeping the requirement forbids, and daily churn would make the tag history noise.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Fetching and refreshing the plugin source is an installer-level operation Claude Code performs; the model has no role in it and cannot cause or block an update.
answers.context_boundary: The whole update mechanism sits outside any model context, at install and session-start time. Only the resulting components, skill metadata, command definitions, hook registrations and MCP schemas, enter a session's window once installed.
answers.lifecycle: An update lands when the marketplace or plugin is refreshed, in practice at a session boundary or an explicit update command, and applies for every subsequent session. It stops when the plugin is disabled or the marketplace entry is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly, which is the cost of the zero-bookkeeping choice. A broken commit on the tracked branch reaches every teammate with nothing to pin back to, and because updates apply at a session boundary the fleet is briefly running several different commits at once. There is also no signal to the user that anything changed, so a hook whose behaviour shifted overnight looks like Claude misbehaving rather than a toolkit update.
answers.version_caveat: Git-repository-backed marketplaces are the normal distribution path for Claude Code plugins, but I cannot confirm from memory whether updates are pulled automatically at session start or require an explicit plugin update invocation, nor the exact command spelling, so I will not assert either. If auto-refresh is not the default, the zero-bookkeeping property holds on the publishing side but consumers still need one command.

answers.primary: A locally launched stdio MCP server acting as an authenticating proxy in front of the internal HTTP service: on each request it shells out to the SSO helper command (or reads its cached token and re-mints when stale), attaches the bearer header, and forwards. Putting the credential logic in a process that runs per call is what survives mid-session expiry.
answers.rejected_alternative: Configuring the internal service directly as an HTTP-transport MCP server with a static Authorization header interpolated from an environment variable. Rejected because the header is resolved once at connect time, so the connection dies the moment the short-lived token expires and only a session restart fixes it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness spawns and supervises the proxy process, but the proxy itself owns the refresh contract. The model owns nothing here and should never see or handle the token.
answers.context_boundary: The proxy is a separate operating-system process with no model context of its own; the SSO helper runs inside it. Only the tool schemas at connect time and the tool results cross into the session window, and the token must be kept out of both, including out of any error message the proxy returns.
answers.lifecycle: The proxy starts when a session with the server configured begins and lives for the session; the token lifecycle is nested inside that, minted or refreshed on demand per call and discarded on process exit. It stops applying when the session ends or the server is removed from configuration.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the right direction: if the SSO helper cannot mint, the tool call errors and nothing happens. The practical problems are that the error surfaces to the model as an opaque tool failure, so it will retry the same call two or three times before reporting, and that if the proxy leaks the raw upstream 401 body it can put credential material into the transcript. A helper that opens an interactive browser or prompts on a terminal will hang the call, since the MCP process has no interactive console.
answers.version_caveat: Environment-variable interpolation in MCP configuration exists in current versions, but I do not know of a native configuration field that runs a command to produce a header value per request, and I am not going to invent one. If such a field does exist in the installed version it would replace the proxy; absent that, the proxy is the mechanism that actually handles mid-session expiry.

answers.primary: Hooks shipped inside the toolkit plugin: a SessionStart hook that launches a detached tailer writing new lines to a spool file, plus a UserPromptSubmit hook that drains the spool and injects the new lines as additional context, with a SessionEnd hook that kills the tailer. The plugin being active is what arms it, so nobody has to ask Claude to start watching.
answers.rejected_alternative: An MCP server exposing a read_error_log tool. Rejected because it is pull, not push: the model only sees log lines when it decides to call the tool, which is exactly the 'someone has to ask' behaviour the requirement rules out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Hook events fire deterministically on session start and on each user prompt regardless of what the model wants, and the injected text arrives whether or not the model asked for it.
answers.context_boundary: The tail process runs outside any model context and the spool file is ordinary disk state. What crosses is the drained log lines, injected into the main session window as additional context at each prompt boundary, which means the model's window absorbs the log volume directly.
answers.lifecycle: It arms at session start whenever the plugin is active and disarms at session end, when the plugin is disabled, or if the tailer dies. Each drain covers the interval since the previous prompt.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, and it does not truly deliver lines 'as they appear'. Injection happens at turn boundaries, so during a long agentic turn nothing surfaces until the next user prompt; a noisy log will blow out the context window across a session and the injection needs a hard line cap and truncation. If the tailer is orphaned it leaks a process per session, and if the hook errors the harness generally continues without it, so the failure is silent.
answers.version_caveat: SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit hook events with a context-injection output exist in current Claude Code, but I do not know the exact minimum version or the precise field name for injected context, so I will not state one. I also cannot confirm any mechanism for genuinely asynchronous mid-turn push into an in-flight context, so the turn-boundary approximation is what I would commit to.

answers.primary: The guarantee has to live in the credential itself, not in Claude Code: provision a read-only credential out of band from the vendor, scoped read at issuance, and configure the hosted integration as a remote MCP server that carries that credential. If the vendor's own sign-in flow cannot be constrained to read scopes, the browser OAuth path is the wrong mechanism here and a vendor-issued restricted token or a read-only service account is.
answers.rejected_alternative: Deny rules in settings.json blocking the write and admin MCP tool names. Rejected because that is a client-side gate on the assistant's behaviour, which is precisely the weaker property the requirement rejects; a misconfigured machine, a renamed tool, or any other client using the same stored token still writes.
answers.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor the harness: the vendor's authorization server owns it, and that is why this design satisfies the requirement. Claude Code is only a carrier for a token whose ceiling was fixed before it ever reached the machine.
answers.context_boundary: The credential lives in the local credential store or environment and must never enter the model's window. Tool schemas cross in at connect time and results cross back; if the vendor advertises write tools they will still appear in the tool list even though calls will be refused upstream.
answers.lifecycle: It applies from the moment the read-only credential is issued until it expires or is revoked, and is re-established on rotation. It stops applying the instant anyone re-runs the interactive sign-in and replaces the stored credential with a broader one, which is the event to guard against.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed upstream: a write attempt returns a 403 from the vendor, so the ceiling holds even if the model is confused or prompt-injected into trying. The realistic breach is re-authorization drift, an engineer hitting the OAuth flow and consenting to the full scope set, so pair the token with a deny rule and a managed settings pin as defence in depth, and audit vendor-side which grants exist rather than trusting the local config.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot confirm that Claude Code lets you constrain the scopes requested during a remote MCP server's OAuth authorization, and I am not going to claim a flag for it. That uncertainty is exactly why I would not rely on the client at all: if scope selection is not controllable, the read-only property must be enforced by the vendor at issuance.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server declared in a .mcp.json file committed at the repository root, pointing at the staging-database tool service, with any secret referenced through environment-variable interpolation rather than written into the file. A fresh clone brings the configuration with it and Claude Code prompts each engineer to approve the project's servers before connecting.
answers.rejected_alternative: Adding the same server at user scope with the MCP CLI. Rejected because a user-scope server follows the engineer into every project they open, which directly violates the requirement that no other repository ever uses this connection.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It discovers the file, gates the connection behind a per-project approval prompt, records the decision locally, and refuses to connect without it; the model cannot self-approve.
answers.context_boundary: The database tool service runs outside the session entirely. On approval the server's tool schemas load into the session window and query results cross back, which matters because a database tool can return very wide result sets and should paginate or cap rows server-side.
answers.lifecycle: It is discovered at the start of every session opened in that repository; the approval is asked once per engineer and then persists in that engineer's local per-project settings. It stops applying outside the repository, if the approval is reset, or if the file is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, and the sticky decline is the practical annoyance: an engineer who dismisses the prompt has no database tools and no obvious path back, because reversing it means resetting the recorded project choices rather than re-triggering the prompt. The other real hazard is a committed credential, since .mcp.json is in version control, so the connection string and password must come from the environment.
answers.version_caveat: Project-scoped .mcp.json with an approval prompt and environment-variable interpolation is standard current behaviour, and I believe there is a CLI command to reset recorded project approvals, but I will not state its exact spelling from memory. Enterprise managed settings can pre-approve or forbid project servers, which would override the per-engineer prompt.

answers.primary: A plugin-shipped SessionStart hook that performs an idempotent first-run install into a stable location keyed to the toolkit's identity rather than to its version or install path, for example a directory under the user's Claude configuration named for the plugin, and skips instantly when a marker matching the current lockfile hash is already present. The location choice is the whole answer: anything installed inside the plugin's own directory is replaceable on update.
answers.rejected_alternative: Vendoring node_modules into the distributed plugin repository. Rejected because it bloats every clone of the marketplace, still lives inside the directory an update replaces, and ships platform-specific native binaries that break on a teammate's different OS or Node version.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the hook on schedule; the install script owns idempotency, the storage location, and the decision to reinstall. The model owns nothing and should not be asked to run installs itself.
answers.context_boundary: The install runs as a subprocess with no model context. Only a short status line should be injected into the session window; piping full npm output into the context is a real and common waste, so the script should be quiet on success and verbose only on failure.
answers.lifecycle: It runs at every session start, no-ops when the marker matches, and does real work on the first run after installation and on any toolkit update that changes the dependency manifest. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled, and the installed tree should then be pruned rather than left behind.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and slowly. A first-run install delays session start by however long npm takes, and on an offline or proxied machine it fails while the session proceeds regardless, so the breakage surfaces much later as an opaque module-not-found from whatever tool needed it. Keying the directory to a version instead of the toolkit name produces the stranding the requirement names, an orphaned tree per release; keying it to the plugin directory produces the wipe. Concurrent sessions starting together can also race on the same install, so a lock file is needed.
answers.version_caveat: SessionStart hooks and a plugin-root environment variable exist in current Claude Code, but I do not know of a native declarative dependency-install lifecycle for plugins, and I will not invent a manifest field for one. If the installed version has such a hook contract it should be preferred over a hand-rolled script; absent that, the idempotent session-start installer with an out-of-tree target directory is the mechanism I would commit to.
